data.title: The UV index is not the warm sensation of sunlight on bare skin
data.author: evakhoury
data.article_summary: 文章指出，阳光的温暖感与晒伤风险并不直接相关。温暖主要来自可见光和红外线加热皮肤，而晒伤主要由紫外线B损伤DNA引起，二者机制和能量强度差异很大。早晚阳光虽暖，紫外线较弱；阴天仍可能晒伤，云隙、雪地反射还会增强紫外线。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：紫外线导致晒伤的生物机制，以及体感温度、环境和UV指数对防晒判断的影响。

不同观点：
• **晒伤机制的科学解释**：Terr_认为晒伤并非“错误DNA制造错误蛋白”直接造成，而是UV损伤DNA后，受损细胞启动自毁并向免疫系统发出信号，引发炎症、清除和癌变风险控制。kens补充了胸腺嘧啶二聚体机制：相邻T碱基被UV连接，虽多数可修复，少数会在复制时形成突变。  
• **体感不能可靠反映UV风险**：GuB-42、lemming指出水面降温、微风或低气温会掩盖UV伤害；新西兰夏季可能“感觉只有20度”，但UV却高于欧洲，因而比炎热地区更难凭感觉控制暴晒。nomel则认为自己能感知防晒霜覆盖差异，并提出用盲测UV光源验证这种感觉。  
• **UV指数与环境判断**：DStiego强调澳大利亚高UV下查看手表指数的重要性；YesBox提到“影子短于身高”可作危险提示，并比较佛蒙特（约6）与德州（11以上）。herf解释正午空气路径较短、散射较少，因此UV更强；avidiax质疑天气应用对阴天UV预报不一致，xattt则怀疑能否凭天空颜色判断UV。  
• **晒太阳时段与维生素D争议**：pazimzadeh反驳“早晚更安全”这一说法，认为低UV时获得足够维生素D与避免红斑之间的窗口更窄，短时间正午曝晒可能更有效，但需结合暴露面积和当地条件。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于“体感热度是否能代表晒伤风险”以及UV指数、云层和季节变化的准确评估；总体共识是不能仅凭温度或阳光强弱判断，应参考UV指数并采取防护。

49808109.article_content:
The UV index is not the warm sensation of sunlight on bare skin
13 Jul, 2026
The warmth of sunlight is not a reliable indicator of how quickly you will sunburn in a given situation. On one hand, you can still get sunburned on a cooler cloudy day, while on the other hand, the sun can feel scorching hot on your skin in the morning and yet you won't sunburn (very quickly).
You probably knew this already, but it still feels unintuitive to me. I'm going to look at numbers and think about them until I convince myself, and perhaps you, that this is true.
How does sunburn happen
Sunburn is triggered when your DNA is damaged from light absorption - in particular, UV-B (and to a limited extent, UV-A) is absorbed in a way that alters DNA's molecular structure
1
.
Image:
DNA UV mutation
by Mouagip (derivative of a NASA / David Herring original), released into the public domain.
This interferes with protein synthesis and wreaks havoc in your body over time, but the DNA damage itself is painless
2
.
Why does the sun feel warm
Sunlight feels warm because visible and infrared light excites vibrational modes in various molecules in your skin, especially water and melanin. For physics reasons, this is strictly a form of heating and never
directly
damages molecular structure.
And if you have a darker skin tone, the sun will
feel
warmer to you, yet you'll sunburn much more slowly.
Visible light, near-IR and mid-IR are absorbed to different degrees and at different depths of the skin, but they all contribute to that feeling of warmth.
Different mechanisms, different scales
Not only are the mechanisms completely different for sunburn and solar heating, the orders of magnitude of energy are as well.
At the Earth's surface, the UV-B band is hundreds of times less intense than near-IR. Reasonably, it takes a lot more power to toast your buns (and the rest of your body) than it does to toast your DNA
3
.
For some reason, knowing this makes it more intuitive to me that sunlight's warmth is disconnected from the rate of sunburn. Even if you were absorbing all that UV-B as heat, the resulting warmth would be completely imperceptible.
Time of day affects UV and IR differently
The sun is by far the most intense when the sun is overhead - solar noon. This is true regardless of wavelength of light. However, UV intensity drops off more rapidly than IR as you get further away from noon, as it gets scattered more heavily by the atmosphere.
So, the sun may still feel pretty intense in the morning or late afternoon, but the risk of sunburn is considerably lower.
Wait, what about the weather?
Clouds are made of water, which scatters UV and absorbs IR. On a uniformly cloudy day, both UV index and perceived warmth from the sun drop substantially. However, if there are gaps in the clouds, it can actually amplify the UV intensity at ground level. Snow and ice contribute to this effect as well.
Where did these plots come from?
These plots are simulated measurements created using
pvlib
, an open-source Python library for modeling solar energy, using its implementation of the
SPECTRL2
model to estimate the spectrum of sunlight reaching the ground throughout the day.
Anderson, K., Hansen, C., Holmgren, W., Jensen, A., Mikofski, M., and Driesse, A. “pvlib python: 2023 project update.” Journal of Open Source Software, 8(92), 5994, (2023). DOI: 10.21105/joss.05994.
Some caveats:
pvlib is designed for solar panels, not human bodies
assumes a perfectly clear sky over Toronto (43.8°N, 79.4°W) on 2026-07-12, with the sun hitting a horizontal object
other model parameters are set to reasonable defaults and do not come from historical measurements
SPECTRL2 cuts off at 300 nm, so UV-C and a part of UV-B are not shown
Ow, my spine!
↩
Your nerve endings may have DNA but your DNA does not have nerve endings!
↩
"Claude, please estimate what percentage of my skin is DNA by weight."
↩

不同观点：
• 渐进戒断派：通过降低烟油浓度、改用尼古丁口香糖或贴片，再逐步延长间隔，通常历时数月甚至一年；过程痛苦，但长期值得，戒后仍可能有 cravings 或相关梦境。  
• “电子烟较易戒”派：认为香烟因快速尼古丁峰值、吸烟仪式及烟雾中的 MAOI 更难戒；电子烟可作为降低危害、摆脱香烟的“梯子”，戒电子烟相对容易。  
• “电子烟更易失控”派：指出甜味电子烟可全天候吸食，强化手口动作和多巴胺刺激，甚至导致中毒；贴片因释放缓慢、缺少仪式感，可能是更优方式。  
• 医疗辅助派：支持使用伐尼克兰等药物，认为临床成功率较高、心理负担较小。  
• 替代烟草派：有人采用鼻烟、嚼烟、瑞典 snus，或建议烟斗、雪茄；也有人讽刺“改吸香烟/种烟草”是错误方向。

补充讨论：争议焦点是电子烟究竟是有效的戒烟工具，还是会制造新的长期成瘾。评论还反驳“尼古丁只是咖啡因”的说法，并强调摄入方式会显著影响依赖性。

data.title: Show HN: Training a model to identify AI web content from structure alone
data.author: jochenmadler
data.article_summary: 论文提出“SlopShape”方法，通过信息组织、证据呈现和写作风格等结构特征识别商业网页中的AI生成内容。研究比较了268家公司2250篇人类博客与五种模型生成的11250篇仿作，利用214项特征实现98.0%的宏F1，即使改写后仍保持98.1%。该方法还能以79.3%准确率归因生成模型，并公开代码与数据。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕“AI slop（低质、无创意的AI生成内容）”识别工具的可靠性、评测方法及其实际意义展开讨论。

不同观点：
• **方法与可复现性质疑**：asdff认为工具过度依赖LLM来设定、审核和检测阈值，再用这些结果训练分类器；自然语言提示存在信息损失，且依赖单一第三方模型和持续的token成本。模型未来可能下线或变化，导致难以复现、迁移和使用不同训练数据，建议改用确定性的代码规则。
• **应测试“人类低质内容”误判**：bryanrasmussen认为，若要证明系统能识别AI slop，必须检验它是否会把人类制造的无聊、低质内容误判为AI。他提出两种测试：使用AI普及前的营销、公文和官僚文本并匿名化；让人类专门仿写AI slop，观察系统能否识别其并非AI生成。
• **对项目目标和社会价值的批判**：pooploop64以讽刺口吻质疑该项目究竟是在帮助AI筛选自身垃圾、提高“垃圾质量”，还是让AI摄入更多自身产物；他认为这可能是一个专门制造信息污染的系统。

补充讨论：争议焦点包括分类标准是否可靠、如何区分“AI生成”与“人类低质文本”，以及该工具是在减少还是扩大内容污染。blackboxdev的评论被标记，未提供可分析的观点。

Title:
SlopShape: Identifying AI-Generated Commercial Web Content
Authors:
Jochen Madler
(Sitefire)
View a PDF of the paper titled SlopShape: Identifying AI-Generated Commercial Web Content, by Jochen Madler (Sitefire)
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Word-level detectors identify unedited AI-generated text almost perfectly, but the literature documents their brittleness under rewording, and a word-level score neither characterizes a text nor identifies which AI model wrote it. We ask whether AI-generated text can be identified one level deeper, from structural signatures: how information is presented, in what order, with what evidence, and in what voice. We replicate StoryScope (Russell et al., 2026), which showed such patterns for AI-generated fiction, on commercial content: 2,250 pre-ChatGPT human blog posts from 268 company domains against 11,250 AI mirrors from five frontier models. A 214-feature instrument, applied by an LLM and validated in a human gold-annotation session (human-human kappa 0.928, human-model 0.946), detects AI posts from its 187 structural features alone at 98.0 macro-F1 on held-out companies, unchanged (98.1) when every AI post is reworded by its own model. The signal characterizes and attributes: AI posts share a tidy, self-announcing shape, 79.3% are attributed to the correct source against a 16.7% chance rate, and human posts occupy rare structural configurations. All effects replicate StoryScope's, consistent in direction and larger in magnitude. We release pipeline, instrument, prompts, code, and aggregate artifacts.

49800566.article_summary: 论文提出“SlopShape”方法，通过信息组织、证据呈现和写作风格等结构特征识别商业网页中的AI生成内容。研究比较了268家公司2250篇人类博客与五种模型生成的11250篇仿作，利用214项特征实现98.0%的宏F1，即使改写后仍保持98.1%。该方法还能以79.3%准确率归因生成模型，并公开代码与数据。
49800566.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕“AI slop（低质、无创意的AI生成内容）”识别工具的可靠性、评测方法及其实际意义展开讨论。

不同观点：
• **方法与可复现性质疑**：asdff认为工具过度依赖LLM来设定、审核和检测阈值，再用这些结果训练分类器；自然语言提示存在信息损失，且依赖单一第三方模型和持续的token成本。模型未来可能下线或变化，导致难以复现、迁移和使用不同训练数据，建议改用确定性的代码规则。
• **应测试“人类低质内容”误判**：bryanrasmussen认为，若要证明系统能识别AI slop，必须检验它是否会把人类制造的无聊、低质内容误判为AI。他提出两种测试：使用AI普及前的营销、公文和官僚文本并匿名化；让人类专门仿写AI slop，观察系统能否识别其并非AI生成。
• **对项目目标和社会价值的批判**：pooploop64以讽刺口吻质疑该项目究竟是在帮助AI筛选自身垃圾、提高“垃圾质量”，还是让AI摄入更多自身产物；他认为这可能是一个专门制造信息污染的系统。

补充讨论：争议焦点包括分类标准是否可靠、如何区分“AI生成”与“人类低质文本”，以及该工具是在减少还是扩大内容污染。blackboxdev的评论被标记，未提供可分析的观点。

data.title: George Lucas Returns to Earth, Bearing Gifts
data.author: surprisetalk
data.article_summary: 卢卡斯叙事艺术博物馆在洛杉矶开放，由乔治·卢卡斯夫妇捐建，建筑造型独特，耗资约10亿美元。馆内展出约1300件作品，涵盖古代艺术、绘画、摄影、漫画、电影道具及《星球大战》藏品，强调人类故事与艺术的联系。博物馆设有影院，免费放映精选影片，整体兼具娱乐性、包容性与文化价值。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕卢卡斯叙事艺术博物馆的独特馆藏、建筑设计、开幕活动及选址展开讨论。

不同观点：
• **高度赞赏其独特性**：评论认为博物馆将诺曼·洛克威尔、弗里达·卡罗等名家作品，与《Doonesbury》《The Far Side》漫画并置；还把西斯廷教堂、《星球大战》Podrace复原场景及实验电影、《Cowboy Bebop》放在同一参观体验中，形成古怪但富有启发性的收藏体系，博物馆本身也成为值得思考的对象。  
• **关注开幕活动的文化影响力**：有人转发开幕晚宴合影，强调现场汇聚了众多明星和不同领域人才，体现博物馆受到好莱坞及艺术界的广泛关注。  
• **对建筑设计进行联想和比较**：有评论认为博物馆图书馆可能借鉴了斯德哥尔摩城市图书馆的主厅，暗示其空间设计具有明显的建筑参考来源。  
• **以个人经历补充卢卡斯相关背景**：有人回忆曾在旧金山湾区一家餐馆偶遇卢卡斯及其妻子，并提到该餐馆近年已永久关闭。  
• **对选址持保留态度**：有人庆幸博物馆最终没有建在旧金山Presidio，表明其可能反对当年的选址方案，涉及环境、城市规划或历史保护争议。

补充讨论：评论整体偏正面，但争议焦点主要在博物馆应如何选址，而非馆藏内容；建筑是否借鉴斯德哥尔摩图书馆则属于推测性讨论。

49787163.article_content:
Appearing like a groun
ded and formidable spaceship, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, bearing gifts of memories and myths, opened its portals to an Earth-bound selection of people (local notables, friends, museum members, and journalists) last week in a welcoming Los Angeles, christened by its benefactors, George Lucas, the producer and director of
Star Wars
fame and fortune, and his financier wife, Mellody Hobson. (The general public opening will be on September 22.)
The architecture of the galactic conceit, with a reported $1 billion price tag, is most definitely different, almost stunningly so: a sculptural, organic form, described as a “cloud” by Ma Yansong, founder of
MAD Architects
, the principal firm in a design team that also included Michael Siegel of
Stantec
and Mia Lehrer of the heralded local landscape firm of
Studio-MLA
.
Moored in the city’s
Exposition Park
on a deftly landscaped 13-acre campus that had previously been a parking lot, the soaring sweep of the five-story museum may look to some like a makeshift sci-fi construct, but its interior is grounded in a familiar labyrinth of accessible galleries and convenient visitor services.
Lucas hesitantly declared at the media preview that the museum, long in planning,
“was created to honor humanity’s stories and the artists who illustrate them” and, in doing so, “connect our modern imaginations with our ancient emotions, creating community.”
The diversity of the roughly 1,300 objects on display—housed in 33 galleries totalling 100,000 square feet—is impressive. It ranges from prehistoric cave paintings, ancient sculptures of gods and goddesses, and Renaissance paintings to screen art, rare vintage illustrations, and photographs. The collection also includes graphic novels and comics, which the museum notes “have not always received the respect they deserve.” Lucas calls them “the people’s art.”
The museum library.
Several exhibits exploring the Skywalker saga should appeal to the young and young-at-heart
Star Wars
fans, weaned as they were through (for now) a dozen feature films. The films, in turn, have generated a seemingly endless Hollywood galaxy of action figures and toys, TV
shows and cartoons, books and video games, clothing, and other themed merchandise far too numerous to mention. (The collective lifetime revenue of
Stars Wars
is estimated to be around $50 billion.)
According to the museum, all of these products are “heavily inspired by archetypes and motifs from classical mythology, religion, political history, and the ‘hero’s journey.’”
Among the exhibits is a selection of vehicle designs, props, costumes, and illustrations from the first six films in the saga that Lucas had, over time, squirreled away for his personal archives. But the museum does way more than commemorate
Star Wars
movies, as some haughty east coast cultural commentators have alluded to in early critiques, out of apparent intellectual and geographic hubris. In contrast, as a longtime fan of comics and cartoons, considerably before being awestruck and enthralled by the masterpieces of art and architecture, I sensed in the engaging exhibits a welcoming curatorial curiosity and refreshing respect for film fans.
The building has two movie theatres.
Indeed, the cinema’s supremacy for telling stories with moving images on a screen is displayed in two theaters on the ground level, off the main lobby, named in honor of
Robert Flaherty
, an acclaimed early documentarian, and
Slavko Vorkapich
, who pioneered special effects and experimental films in the analog heyday of Hollywood, before CGI took over. Not coincidentally, he briefly was also the chair of the famed USC Department of Film, which Lucas attended. To entice, the theaters will each operate free to museumgoers as open-door venues, screening curated films continuously.
The galleries also include a wealth of still photography by luminaries such as Robert Capra, Gordon Parks, Alfred Eisenstaedt, and Dorothea Lange; illustrations by Maxwell Parrish, Norman Rockwell, Andrew and N.C. Wyeth, Frank Frazetta; paintings and murals by Diego Rivera, Judith Baca, and Thomas Hart Benton; and rare comic books illustrated by a bevy of artists: Mœbius, Marie Severin, Jack Kirby, Alison Bechdel, Jim Lee, Frank Miller, Rafael Navarro, and R. Crumb.
Eclectic as the galleries may be, the design of the public areas
are blandly functional,
and the circulation thankfully fluid, even to this mobility-challenged critic—though more seating, as always, would be appreciated. But there is little question that the museum itself is a good fit for Los Angeles, however bruised it is as the entertainment capital of the world. Certainly the museum feels more at home here than it would have been in Chicago, where it was initially to be located until Lucas failed to get the site he wanted on the lakefront. (He was similarly thwarted in San Francisco,
when civic leaders balked at putting the museum in the Presidio.)

data.title: Obscura: VPN that can't log your activity
data.author: Flimm
data.article_summary: 文章介绍隐私型VPN服务Obscura。与传统VPN可同时掌握用户身份和浏览记录不同，Obscura采用分离式架构：仅见连接IP，不记录；流量经WireGuard端到端加密，出口节点由独立的Mullvad运行，无法关联用户身份。服务支持匿名账号、闪电网络和Monero付款，采用较难封锁的QUIC隐身协议，并开放源代码供验证。月费8美元，每账户最多5个同时连接。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Obscura通过两跳架构分离用户IP与访问目标，试图减少VPN提供商单方面掌握完整活动记录，并提升隐私与反审查能力。

不同观点：
• 认可其技术思路：第一跳只见IP，第二跳只见目标网站，类似Apple Private Relay、Tor、多跳VPN、OHTTP及VP.net；与Mullvad合作、可验证内层WireGuard连接，以及免邮箱和随机账号注册，被认为是积极信号。  
• 质疑创新性与宣传：有人认为这只是成熟的多跳隐私方案；“首个无法记录活动的VPN”被指不实，Zero Knowledge Systems等早有类似实践。  
• 质疑信任模型：即使Obscura和Mullvad分开运行，仍可能事后串联日志；用户必须相信双方不会合谋。有人还追问VPN出口端是否仍能看到未加密流量、流量填充和检测页如何区分用户。  
• 产品比较意见：质疑为何不直接选择更成熟、信誉更高且客户端完全开源的Mullvad。  
• 其他反馈：注册流程受好评但安装有错误；网站视觉风格被批评为像素化元素与圆角方形缺乏统一；另有人提醒资金可能流向存在争议的方面。

补充讨论：争议核心是Obscura的实际新增隐私保障、合谋风险及其宣传是否夸大；评论也在讨论透明度、开源程度和产品成熟度。

主要讨论点：Obscura通过两跳架构分离用户IP与访问目标，试图减少VPN提供商单方面掌握完整活动记录，并提升隐私与反审查能力。

不同观点：
• 认可其技术思路：第一跳只见IP，第二跳只见目标网站，类似Apple Private Relay、Tor、多跳VPN、OHTTP及VP.net；与Mullvad合作、可验证内层WireGuard连接，以及免邮箱和随机账号注册，被认为是积极信号。  
• 质疑创新性与宣传：有人认为这只是成熟的多跳隐私方案；“首个无法记录活动的VPN”被指不实，Zero Knowledge Systems等早有类似实践。  
• 质疑信任模型：即使Obscura和Mullvad分开运行，仍可能事后串联日志；用户必须相信双方不会合谋。有人还追问VPN出口端是否仍能看到未加密流量、流量填充和检测页如何区分用户。  
• 产品比较意见：质疑为何不直接选择更成熟、信誉更高且客户端完全开源的Mullvad。  
• 其他反馈：注册流程受好评但安装有错误；网站视觉风格被批评为像素化元素与圆角方形缺乏统一；另有人提醒资金可能流向存在争议的方面。

补充讨论：争议核心是Obscura的实际新增隐私保障、合谋风险及其宣传是否夸大；评论也在讨论透明度、开源程度和产品成熟度。

data.title: 16-bit Intel 8088 chip (c. 1985)
data.author: rbanffy
data.article_summary: 文章介绍布考斯基诗歌《Follow》：诗中罗列早期电脑、操作系统和磁盘格式彼此不兼容的荒谬，讽刺技术竞争、商业壁垒及人造系统的繁琐。随后笔锋转向萨凡纳的风与火鸡秃鹰求偶，突出自然运行自如、恒久不变，以此反衬人类科技的混乱与徒劳。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕布考斯基一首涉及早期计算机兼容性问题的诗，评论者同时讨论其文学价值、技术准确性及复古计算机体验。

不同观点：
• 文学欣赏：PaulHoule、jojocool0501和runjake推荐布考斯基的诗集、小说及书信，强调他也写猫、赛马、饮酒等日常生活；有人引用“没有完全浪费一生本身就是成就”。
• 时代记录：badc0ffee认为这首诗是对当年计算机现实的“事实观察”，体现不同MS-DOS机器之间不兼容造成的困扰；runjake因亲历当时的技术陷阱而产生共鸣。
• 技术补充：Luc指出“Commodore 64无法读取IBM PC文件”并非绝对：1571驱动器硬件已具备读取IBM软盘的能力，后来软件Big Blue Reader才逐步实现；rzzzt补充1581也有一定MFM软盘兼容性。
• 复古计算机立场：有人提到Tandy 2000等非PC兼容机如今令复古玩家失望，但仍对AT&T 6300、DEC Rainbow、Zenith Z-100等机器感兴趣。

补充讨论：部分评论从诗歌转向作者作品推荐和个人收藏经历；另有人发现相关域名确实用于诗歌，并非因名称而联想到的其他主题。争议焦点主要是诗中关于磁盘兼容性的表述是否过于绝对，实际取决于驱动器型号和软件支持。

49803635.article_content:
Charles Bukowski
Follow
16-bit Intel 8088 chip
with an Apple Macintosh
you can't run Radio Shack programs
in its disc drive.
nor can a Commodore 64
drive read a file
you have created on an
IBM Personal Computer.
both Kaypro and Osborne computers use
the CP/M operating system
but can't read each other's
handwriting
for they format (write
on) discs in different
ways.
the Tandy 2000 runs MS-DOS but
can't use most programs produced for
the IBM Personal Computer
unless certain
bits and bytes are
altered
but the wind still blows over
Savannah
and in the Spring
the turkey buzzard struts and
flounces before his
hens.
© by owner. provided at no charge for educational purposes
Read more →
Analysis (
hide
)
Places tech's petty squabbles next to timeless nature.
It pits the frustrating, proprietary world of early personal computing against the unchanging rituals of the natural world, a classic move for this writer who always found the eternal in the gutter.
Form mirrors the fragmented tech landscape.
The short, abrupt lines and jarring line breaks feel like a system error or a jammed disk drive, a blunt formal experiment compared to his usually raw but fluid lines about bars and racetracks.
A sneer at capitalist nonsense masked as progress.
The whole poem lists incompatible systems, echoing his lifelong disgust with any system - be it jobs, government, or now, consumer tech - designed to trap and frustrate the ordinary person.
The punchline is pure, old-school him.
After the tech rant, the switch to the turkey buzzard is classic: a crude, ugly bird performing a mating ritual is the
real
, unchanging operating system, undercutting all the human silliness that came before.
It reads like a prophecy for today's walled gardens.
Written in the early days, it perfectly predicts our modern frustrations with incompatible apps, operating systems, and digital ecosystems, making a 40-year-old poem feel ripped from a current tech forum. (ai)

data.title: Launch HN: Coverage Cat (YC S22) – Umbrella insurance via your personal agent
data.author: botacode
data.article_summary: Coverage Cat是一家持牌保险经纪平台，帮助用户比较房屋、雨伞、汽车和租客保险，强调价格透明、隐私保护、不出售客户线索，并提供人工经纪支持。平台覆盖加州、佛州、纽约州、德州和华盛顿州，支持AI引导投保、保费估算、方案比较、理赔指导及面向开发者的API接入。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：新保险产品的定位、报价能力、用户隐私与保险稳定性，以及产品覆盖范围和介绍方式。

不同观点：
• 隐私与稳定性担忧：skyberrys想在加州购买房屋险，但担心个人信息被转卖导致骚扰，也担心房屋临海、风险较高，新保险公司一年后拒保或涨价。  
• 雨伞险的价值存在分歧：mannyv认为雨伞险通常是车险、房险的附加产品，保险公司会设置保额门槛，且有未成年子女驾驶时投保复杂；dgacmu则认为通过GEICO/Travelers购买已很方便、价格也不高，没必要大幅比价。  
• 报价与商业模式：曾参与Policygenius开发的DeltaCoast关注如何在用户少填资料的情况下获得准确报价，以及用户每年重新比价但保险公司不愿为“流失客户”付费的矛盾。  
• 产品覆盖不足：cruffle_duffle指出其主要支出是车险，而工具不支持；自己是租客，只需要租客险，因此认为产品实际无用，且支持范围不够清晰。  
• 其他功能诉求：abirch询问是否计入伯克希尔股东的GEICO、房屋及雨伞险折扣。  
• 信息表达：hnlmorg认为产品介绍过长，读者难以迅速理解核心功能，建议精简。

补充讨论：有人误把“umbrella insurance”理解为日常雨伞险，反映名称可能造成理解障碍；jtap则基于保险行业经验表示支持并愿意交流。争议焦点主要是雨伞险是否值得专门比价，以及该产品的覆盖范围和用户价值是否足够广。

data.title: The JavaScript Midlife Crisis
data.author: maroun-baydoun
data.article_summary: 文章回顾了 JavaScript 从浏览器脚本发展为覆盖前后端及多种设备的通用语言。尽管它曾饱受诟病，也不断面临替代者和工具链重写的挑战，但凭借生态庞大、跨平台、开源免费及开发者熟悉度，JavaScript始终难以被取代。如今工具链更快，却也让开发者逐渐忽视语言本身的优势。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：JavaScript 工具链及应用是否应被 Rust、Go、Zig、WebAssembly 等更高性能技术替代，以及速度、可维护性和适用场景之间的权衡。

不同观点：
• **反对过度迁移到 Rust 等语言**：Klonoar 认为重写 bundler 虽提升速度，却缩小了 JavaScript 开发者的维护和贡献群体，开源项目也可能因技术门槛上升而变成“黑箱”。反方则认为关键基础设施本就不应由能力不足者维护，学习新语言不是不可逾越的障碍。  
• **支持采用高性能语言**：nzoschke 认为 Rust、Go、Zig 正逐渐接管 JS 工具链乃至应用开发；JS 在语言一致性、标准库和性能方面存在缺陷，因此倾向 Go+HTMX、减少 JS 和构建工具。Kuyawa 则按场景选择：桌面应用用 Rust/Zig/Swift，简单 CRUD 用原生 HTML/CSS/JS，游戏和极致优化场景用 Wasm。  
• **性能至关重要**：cisc 举例称 Google Sheets 和 Amazon Prime Video 使用 WebAssembly 后性能约提升一倍，认为 Wasm 能让 Java、Rust 等语言进入浏览器。  
• **为 JavaScript 辩护或提出限制**：msteffen 指出 V8、LuaJIT 等 JIT 运行时可能达到甚至超过部分编译语言；spankalee 认为 JS 语言本身并非全盘糟糕，但其高度动态性使 Wasm、低延迟和高吞吐场景更困难。  
• **极端反 JS 立场**：hn_submit 将 JS 视为低效、臃肿的根源；hackersnooze 简化为“解释型语言必然比编译型慢”。  
• **多语言学习观点**：tannerr_dev 认为学习 Go 能改变编程思维，不必只精通一种语言。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于性能收益是否足以抵消维护门槛、生态和开发效率损失，以及 JS 的问题究竟源于语言本身还是工具实现质量。

49807248.article_content:
Holding on to the crown?
You could improve it, hide it, compile to it or complain about it. You just couldn't get rid of it.
A while back, I made a half-observation, half-joke on
LinkedIn
.
The great JavaScript toolchain rewrite barged in. The older tools that helped cement the language's place in our stacks became uncool, if not suspicious. Their sluggish performance took the blame for slowing down millions of lines of code on their way to production. It's increasingly difficult to keep track of the cool kids on the block. Their names might not be catchy, but their promise is captivating: speed, and a lot of it.
It's a strange time to be a JavaScript developer. The language has never been more ubiquitous, yet it seems to be losing ground in its own backyard. The tools are faster, the setup easier, the abstractions thicker. We write, configure and wait less. We bundle, ship and hotfix more. What happens between our code and the end product becomes easier to ignore.
The benchmarks are all beaming green. The line charts are trending up, down, or sideways—whichever direction means fewer calls at 3 AM. So why am I here to ruin the party?
The language that wouldn't die
For a language (in)famously written in ten days, JavaScript managed to achieve the unthinkable. It escaped its birthplace, the browser, and started swallowing everything around it. The reaction was predictable:
Who in their right mind would write their server and tools in JavaScript?
It turned out, many many many would. JavaScript made it onto phones, gaming consoles, microcontrollers and your fridge. If it understands bits, it can run JavaScript.
Despite its popularity, JavaScript never had it easy. Not long after its inception, attempts to fix, or rather replace it altogether, were already in motion. Microsoft endowed Internet Explorer with VBScript and JScript, their own JavaScript flavour—not to be confused with J-Pop and JRPGs. In the 90s, everything sounded cooler if it started with J. Macromedia, and later Adobe, littered the internet with Flash intros and games powered by ActionScript. Google bet on Dart for the future of Chrome before relegating it to Flutter.
Projects such as CoffeeScript added some syntactic sugar to the JavaScript cup. When we weren't trying to replace JavaScript, we were busy patching it from the outside. jQuery unified a web platform whose browsers were barely on speaking terms. Lodash filled glaring gaps in the language's arrays and objects. Moment.js made dates somebody else's problem.
JavaScript wasn't sitting still while everyone plotted its demise, either. Within its single thread, it was rather busy. Browser vendors, standards bodies and the community kept pushing the language forward. ECMAScript releases brought long awaited language features. TC39 kept the proposals coming, and browsers slowly learned to agree on what JavaScript was supposed to do. Over time, its standard library became less embarrassingly sparse.
Then came TypeScript, and JavaScript's head was finally on a silver platter. Or so it seemed. TypeScript succeeded where the others failed by accepting one inconvenient truth: JavaScript wasn't going anywhere.
You could improve it, hide it, compile to it or complain about it. You just couldn't get rid of it.
The superpower we're giving away
One language to rule them all is both a blessing and a curse. We spent decades talking about the curse. Somewhere along the way, we forgot about the blessing.
As JavaScript continued to spread, it started eating its own dog food. Node.js enabled a slew of tools to emerge and conquer the ecosystem. Linters, bundlers, formatters and test runners were speaking the same language as the code they linted, bundled, formatted and tested.
If, or rather when, something broke in that toolchain, the average JavaScript developer would be able to check the code. Maybe they'd understand the bug. If they'd had their eight hours of sleep, maybe they'd fix it. If they were feeling combative, maybe they'd submit a pull request. At the very least, they knew enough of the language to confidently blame the bug on the maintainers.
And that familiarity travelled surprisingly well. The same language followed developers from the browser to the server, and eventually almost everywhere in between. JavaScript accelerated the rise of full-stack engineers, or perhaps full-ecosystem engineers. Whether anyone can truly master both ends of the stack without achieving demigod status is a discussion for another day. But JavaScript made the transition considerably easier. Engineers could bring along their knowledge of the call stack, prototype-based inheritance and the unfortunate fact that
typeof null === "object"
to almost any project.
People built entire careers and businesses around this catch-all ecosystem. The fact that most of it was and continues to be open source and
free
certainly helps.
JavaScript won the browser wars, and several key battles elsewhere. Then Rust and friends showed up for
49807248.article_summary: 文章回顾了 JavaScript 从浏览器脚本发展为覆盖前后端及多种设备的通用语言。尽管它曾饱受诟病，也不断面临替代者和工具链重写的挑战，但凭借生态庞大、跨平台、开源免费及开发者熟悉度，JavaScript始终难以被取代。如今工具链更快，却也让开发者逐渐忽视语言本身的优势。
49807248.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：JavaScript 工具链及应用是否应被 Rust、Go、Zig、WebAssembly 等更高性能技术替代，以及速度、可维护性和适用场景之间的权衡。

不同观点：
• **反对过度迁移到 Rust 等语言**：Klonoar 认为重写 bundler 虽提升速度，却缩小了 JavaScript 开发者的维护和贡献群体，开源项目也可能因技术门槛上升而变成“黑箱”。反方则认为关键基础设施本就不应由能力不足者维护，学习新语言不是不可逾越的障碍。  
• **支持采用高性能语言**：nzoschke 认为 Rust、Go、Zig 正逐渐接管 JS 工具链乃至应用开发；JS 在语言一致性、标准库和性能方面存在缺陷，因此倾向 Go+HTMX、减少 JS 和构建工具。Kuyawa 则按场景选择：桌面应用用 Rust/Zig/Swift，简单 CRUD 用原生 HTML/CSS/JS，游戏和极致优化场景用 Wasm。  
• **性能至关重要**：cisc 举例称 Google Sheets 和 Amazon Prime Video 使用 WebAssembly 后性能约提升一倍，认为 Wasm 能让 Java、Rust 等语言进入浏览器。  
• **为 JavaScript 辩护或提出限制**：msteffen 指出 V8、LuaJIT 等 JIT 运行时可能达到甚至超过部分编译语言；spankalee 认为 JS 语言本身并非全盘糟糕，但其高度动态性使 Wasm、低延迟和高吞吐场景更困难。  
• **极端反 JS 立场**：hn_submit 将 JS 视为低效、臃肿的根源；hackersnooze 简化为“解释型语言必然比编译型慢”。  
• **多语言学习观点**：tannerr_dev 认为学习 Go 能改变编程思维，不必只精通一种语言。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于性能收益是否足以抵消维护门槛、生态和开发效率损失，以及 JS 的问题究竟源于语言本身还是工具实现质量。

data.title: Z80 REPL (2018)
data.author: adunk
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Z80 汇编语言 REPL 的创意、使用体验与功能改进建议。

不同观点：
• 怀旧与历史对比：有人回忆 Apple II Plus 因加入自动启动功能而移除了 Monitor ROM 中的迷你汇编器；相比之下，保留了反汇编器。这种迷你汇编器被认为是早期接近“汇编语言 REPL”的工具。  
• 项目价值认可：评论者指出该项目源码其实已存在约 8 年，但仍认为让人能够即时输入、运行和反馈 Z80 指令的想法很有趣。  
• 交互缺陷反馈：当前 REPL 似乎无法正确处理无操作数指令后的空格，例如带尾随空格的 `nop` 会被识别为未知指令；这被视为需要修复的解析问题。  
• 自动补全建议：希望可以像 fish shell 一样，仅按 Tab 就循环选择补全项，而不必继续输入指令，按 Enter 确认选择，以提升汇编输入效率。  
• 学习与熟练度：即时反馈能帮助用户迅速恢复对 Z80 汇编语法和指令的“肌肉记忆”。  
• 内容扩展建议：有人希望提供可直接加载到内存中的示例程序，方便体验和学习。

补充讨论：主要争议不在项目理念，而在当前输入解析和补全交互仍不够完善；整体评论基调积极，集中于怀旧价值、实用体验和后续改进方向。

data.title: Claude Code reads AGENTS.md only when telemetry is on
data.author: pszypowicz
data.article_summary: 文章指出，Claude Code 的 AGENTS.md 支持受远程功能开关控制；关闭遥测或非必要流量时，开关无法获取，文件会被静默跳过，且设置为 0 也无效。问题同样影响第三方网关及 Bedrock、Vertex。可通过在 CLAUDE.md 中写入“@AGENTS.md”绕过。作者认为本地文件读取不应依赖遥测，并建议提供警告及全局 AGENTS.md、共享技能支持。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Claude Code 对 AGENTS.md 的读取是否受遥测（telemetry）开关控制，以及这一设计暴露出的发布、隐私和工程质量问题。

不同观点：
• 官方解释：这是为支持远程关闭功能而设置的发布遗留物；关闭遥测会失去相关数据，导致该功能被错误地绑在遥测开关上。已承认是人为失误，并将在 v2.1.281 修复。  
• 工程合理性观点：功能旗标用于将“部署代码”和“启用功能”分离，是常见的分布式系统发布策略；用户不能假设读取 AGENTS.md 永远无害，因为仓库指令可能产生意外影响。  
• 批评观点：功能旗标与遥测本可分离，有人质疑 Anthropic 的工程能力，并担心 AI 生成补丁层层堆叠、缺乏人工审查会造成隐蔽且严重的 bug；也有人联想到 VSCode 强行添加 Copilot 提交署名的问题。  
• 用户体验与隐私观点：AGENTS.md 不应被遥测开关控制；遥控功能同样要求开启遥测，引发对用户控制权和默认行为的担忧。部分用户甚至无法判断这是设计还是 bug。  

补充讨论：CLAUDE.md 存在时可能默认不读取 AGENTS.md，需切换设置才能同时读取；有人建议在 CLAUDE.md 中显式引用 AGENTS.md。另有用户报告 v2.1.280 已无此问题，可能说明修复已提前上线。

49814947.article_content:
Claude Code 2.1.277 announced support for
AGENTS.md
. In a project with no
CLAUDE.md
, it is supposed to read
AGENTS.md
instead. I keep telemetry off in my shell, and in my repos the file never loaded.
Issue #95690
explains why, and I added
my own measurements
to it. This post collects them in one place.
Where the gate is
The loader ships as a built-in plugin called
agents-md
. Its registration in the 2.1.280 bundle looks like this:
var
W
=
!
1
;
var
B
=
()
=>
Oa
(
"tengu_agents_md_mod"
,
W
);
var
H
=
"AGENTS.md as project instructions: by default loaded where the project has no CLAUDE.md; ..."
;
W
is the plugin’s
isOnByDefault
value and it is
false
.
B
is
isAvailable
, and it asks a remote feature flag called
tengu_agents_md_mod
, with
false
as the fallback. When Claude Code cannot fetch the flag, the plugin is unavailable, and the local file is never read. Reading a markdown file from the working directory needs no network at all, but here it waits on a server-side switch.
How I tested it
I made an empty directory that holds only an
AGENTS.md
with a canary word in it, and asked
claude -p
for the word. Each setup ran in two sessions, because the first session in a new configuration only fetches the flag and the second one uses it.
echo
'The canary word is PERIWINKLE.'
> AGENTS.md
claude -p
'What is the canary word from the project instructions? Answer NONE if you have none. Do not read files.'
What I measured
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1
blocks the feature, as the issue says.
DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1
blocks it too. With either variable set,
AGENTS.md
never loaded, so I had to clear both.
Setting either variable to
0
does not help. The block stays in place. The environment variable docs say that any value counts, but that is easy to miss when you try to turn a feature on.
An
env
block in the project’s
.claude/settings.json
that clears both variables has no effect. There is no way to turn the feature on for a single repo.
A session-level override does work from the second session on:
claude --settings
'{"env":{"DISABLE_TELEMETRY":"","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC":""}}'
None of these cases print a warning. The session starts, the model answers without the project instructions, and nothing tells you that a file was skipped. The issue also points out that third-party gateways, Bedrock and Vertex have the same problem, because the flag cannot resolve to true there either.
The workaround
CLAUDE.md
supports
@path
imports, and those do not depend on the flag. A one-line
CLAUDE.md
next to the
AGENTS.md
loads it with telemetry off:
echo
'@AGENTS.md'
> CLAUDE.md
With that file in place, the same canary test returns the word with
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1
still set. The cost is one extra file per repo, which is what the
AGENTS.md
support was supposed to remove.
Why I think this is unacceptable
I turned telemetry off on purpose, and I expect that choice to cost me some diagnostics and nothing else. Here it silently costs me a feature that reads a file from my own disk. A remote flag can make sense for a feature that talks to a server, but the only input this one needs is already in the working directory.
The gate also hits the people who are most likely to care about
AGENTS.md
. Someone who keeps one instruction file for several agents is usually careful about what each tool sends home, and teams on Bedrock, Vertex or a gateway often disable nonessential traffic by policy. They all get a feature that is announced as available and then does nothing.
The silence is the worst part. I confirmed the cause with a canary word and a string search through the binary, and most people will not do that. They will conclude that the model ignores their instructions, and they will spend time on prompts when the file never reached the model in the first place.
A privacy setting should never quietly switch off unrelated local behavior. If Anthropic wants a staged rollout, the fallback for a flag that cannot be fetched should be the documented behavior, or at least a visible message that says what was skipped and why.
What I would like to see
Reading a local file should not depend on telemetry. If the gate has to stay for a gradual rollout, a startup warning when an
AGENTS.md
is present and skipped would save people the time I spent on a canary test.
A global
AGENTS.md
. The plugin looks for
AGENTS.md
and
.claude/AGENTS.md
in project directories only, and there is no user-level file next to the user
CLAUDE.md
. Codex reads a global
~/.codex/AGENTS.md
, and the
/import
command in Claude Code can copy it into the user
CLAUDE.md
, but the copy does not follow later edits. If you keep one set of personal instructions for several agents, you still need an
@
import in the user
CLAUDE.md
that points at the shared file.
Native support for shared agent skills. Codex reads skills from
.agents/skills
in the project and from
~/.agents/skills
in the home directory. Claude Code 2.1.280 knows those paths only in
/i

data.title: Stripe built its internal AI platform
data.author: ltononro
data.article_summary: 文章介绍了Stripe的Knowledge AI Platform及其Agent Foundation团队，重点探讨如何整合和管理知识，使AI系统更准确地理解Stripe产品与开发者文档，并将API变更高效传递到开发者产品中，从而提升AI能力、开发效率和用户体验。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕企业自建、管理型智能体平台的价值、技术路线及产品定位展开讨论，并涉及界面设计和品牌命名。

不同观点：
• 支持者认为，这是企业未来的重要方向：在本地部署受治理的平台，让不同团队使用接近编程智能体能力、但更可控的内部智能体；有人还以开源项目 Lightspeed 呼应这一趋势。  
• 质疑者认为，项目没有解释为何不采用 LangChain、BionicGPT 等现有开源方案，企业重复自建可能缺乏必要性；也有人指出许多有工程资源的公司都在开发类似 Cloudflare OS 的内部系统。  
• 对产品定位存在争议：名为“Knowledge AI Platform”，但评论者未看到知识管理所需的核验、透明度等具体能力，认为它更像通用 Agent 构建器，名称可能只是为内部开发寻找正当性。  
• 有人分享了自建经验：用智能体管理财务、客户、合同、账单、工时等信息，并通过 MCP 连接系统，说明企业内部自动化确有实际需求。  
• 负面评价认为相关宣传夸大，甚至将其与 Spotify“节省 90% token”等说法类比，批评行业“什么都敢说”；另有评论以嘲讽方式批评 LangChain。

补充讨论：部分评论与功能无关，集中于产品名“Kai”引发的新生儿命名玩笑，以及无限滚动、行距、文字过多、缺少暗色模式等网页体验问题。

• 负面评价认为相关宣传夸大，甚至将其与 Spotify“节省 90% token”等说法类比，批评行业“什么都敢说”；另有评论以嘲讽方式批评 LangChain。

补充讨论：部分评论与功能无关，集中于产品名“Kai”引发的新生儿命名玩笑，以及无限滚动、行距、文字过多、缺少暗色模式等网页体验问题。

data.author: mooreds

data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕事故复盘中，管理者应优先追问“发生了什么、为什么发生”，还是直接聚焦“如何避免再次发生”，以及这种沟通方式对领导力、问责和组织改进的影响。

不同观点：
• 支持“先谈改进”：SVP并非推卸责任，而是默认团队基于当时信息做了合理决定，避免复盘变成追责或同理心式的自我辩护，直接要求提出风险缓解和改进方案；这体现了从责怪个人转向改进系统的成熟管理。
• 质疑忽略细节：完全信任团队并不等于无需了解后续方案；若不掌握事故细节，就无法判断改进措施是否合理。领导者应兼顾自上而下与自下而上的信息，关注一线实际。
• 强调两者不可分割：事故经过、影响和“为什么”是制定有效措施的基础，把“原因分析”和“改进方案”对立起来会造成逻辑冲突。管理者若承担问责，就必须了解细节。
• 关注表达方式：即使意图正确，“我不想听细节”也可能显得冷漠、伤人。更好的说法是先肯定团队在当时条件下做了最佳判断，再询问未来如何改变。
• 改进方法论：持续改进不能只不断增加规则和告警，还应审查并删除无效流程；复杂事故通常有多个“促成因素”，不应机械追求单一“根因”。

补充讨论：评论还指出，复盘通常应包含时间线、影响、原因分析和行动项；事故中告警泛滥等系统性问题尤其需要详细调查。争议核心是“聚焦行动”与“理解事实”之间的优先级，以及领导者应在多大程度上介入细节。

49815466.article_content:
A few months ago I was dragged into a call with my engineering counterpart and their boss (who happens to be our SVP of engineering). Something had gone wrong that shouldn't have. Nothing catastrophic, but important enough that I was now on a call with an SVP.
I started to explain how it happened when they cut me off with "Michael, I don't want the details".
They continued:
I know that if we get into the details, the reasons will be perfectly reasonable. You'll explain what happened, I'll understand why everyone made the decisions they made, and I'll empathise with you.
Then it'll happen again.
So I don't want the details. I want to know what we're changing.
At first I thought "I don't want the details" sounded dismissive. How can they make informed decisions without understanding the details?
Then I realised that "I don't want the details" wasn't being dismissive. The executive assumed that we were competent, and was saying "I already believe you. Now let's talk about what happens next".
Asking the right question
After something goes wrong, most organizations ask "Why did this happen?" This is a question we're all familiar with answering.
We write up timelines. We reconstruct decisions. We explain dependencies. At the end of it, we hand over a document that contains the specific combination of events that led to the incident.
Everyone nods their head, says "that makes sense", and we all move on with our day.
Understanding an issue is not the same as fixing it. A good explanation can make things worse. Once everyone agrees that the behaviour was reasonable, the urgency to change anything disappears.
When an incident is an unfortunate but understandable sequence of events where no-one is at fault nothing changes. Then the same thing happens six months later, and everyone is left wondering how we landed here again.
To drive change in your organization, don't ask "why did this happen?".
Instead, ask:
What are we changing so that the same class of failure is less likely next time?
Reasonable people
The SVP wasn't interested in understanding how the issue happened or who was involved. They didn't want to be convinced that everyone involved behaved reasonably. That's a baseline expectation.
Their question became:
“Given that reasonable people produced this outcome, what needs to change?”
Consider these examples:
"We missed it because Alice was on holiday and Bob thought the Widgets team owned it".
Okay. How do we make ownership unambiguous when someone is unavailable?
"The requirements changed three days before launch."
Of course they did! What happens when requirements change inside the launch window?
"The alert fired, but the on-call engineer had already dealt with twenty low-value alerts that evening".
Makes sense. How do we improve the signal to noise ratio of our alerts?
Focus on changing the system. The people are usually not what needs changing.
A good explanation is not a fix
If your postmortem is full of sentences like "we should involve support earlier" and "we need to communicate better", or my personal favourite, "we'll be more careful next time", you have a collection of hopes dressed up as progress.
If your corrective action depends on people remembering a conversation from six months ago, you don't have a corrective action. You have organizational folklore. If everyone involved in the incident left the company tomorrow, would the fix still work? If the answer is
no
, the people may have learned something while the system is still destined to fail.
For a postmortem to drive lasting change, ask:
If the same situation happened tomorrow, what would cause a different outcome?
A process that forces a decision at this point is an improvement. A system that prevents this class of mistake is stronger still.
Process for process' sake
You can take "the system prevents this class of mistake" too far.
Not every failure deserves a new process. That's how you build environments that no-one wants to work in. Sometimes the cost of preventing recurrence is higher than the cost of occasionally accepting the failure, and that's ok.
But you need to accept failure with your eyes open. "We are consciously accepting this risk" is very different from "we said we'd try harder and everyone felt better".
Trust
I still think about what the SVP said a lot. What sounded like impatience was a declaration of trust. They didn't need me to prove that the people involved were competent or well intentioned. They were willing to start there. If the investigation showed otherwise, we could deal with that separately.
What they didn't want was for empathy to become the mechanism by which the organisation absolved itself of having to change.
People are usually making the best decisions they can with the information, incentives and constraints around them. That's why fixing the people is often the wrong answer.
Sometimes the most useful thing a leader can say is:
I believe you. I don’t need the details. Tell me what we're changing.

data.author: bashbjorn
data.article_summary: 文章以戏谑方式介绍“Jev”：用约25行Python加载本地GGUF大模型，根据提示中的选项读取各标签的logits，并通过softmax计算概率，实现邮件分类。该方法快速、无需联网、保护隐私，但只是简化演示，并非完整的Jev系统；文末提供了更完整的开源实现。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕用大模型进行分类、读取 token 概率的方法是否可靠，以及该方案与 Jev 的技术定位、性能和宣传方式。

不同观点：
• **结构化输出优于直接读取 logprobs**：sigmoid10 认为聊天模型可能生成完整解释，导致“A/B/C”概率被稀释；建议使用明确系统提示，或直接输出“Legitimate/Spam/Phishing”等预定义选项。结构化输出还能保留推理过程，但模型自报的概率也未必比 logprobs 更可靠。  
• **logprobs 的可靠性存在争议**：armcat 指出本地模型读取 token 概率尚可，但 GPT-4o 等前沿模型上已基本失效；在置信度评估中，让模型直接表达置信度反而可能与真实置信度相关性更高。  
• **提示设计可改善分类**：antirez 认为先放选项、再放待分析文本，可利用因果注意力让模型更早聚焦任务；加入示例或重复任务与标签也有助于校准。  
• **Jev 的定位和优势不清晰**：bruhhhhhh 质疑 Jev 是否只是更快的专用小模型；分类任务本可由 BERT 等经典模型更快完成，类型安全也能通过结构化输出解决。其他评论要求补充延迟、算力、错误率及输出格式稳定性，才能证明优势。  
• **宣传与内容可信度受质疑**：多位评论者认为文章像营销或讽刺，结尾推广产品又称“parody”，容易误导；“25 行 Python”被讽刺为“import Solution/画个圈再导入猫头鹰”。  
• **概念表述遭批评**：alun 认为 Jev 将自动分类包装成“System One”并不准确，人类通常用“System Two”处理分类，纯逻辑自动执行反而更接近快速反应。

补充讨论：有人认可该方法可作为本地 prompt router，根据任务复杂度选择不同模型；也有人指出，即使方案本身有效，若比 Jev 慢很多，就不能笼统称为“快”。

不同观点：
• [fuzzumms] 认为这种机制是为自动化决策提供某种安全保障的有趣方法，但未展开具体实现方式。

补充讨论：评论整体持积极但审慎的探索态度，主要争议或未决焦点不在理念本身，而在于任务边界能否成功实施、如何进行治理，以及能否有效防止自动化代理越界和失控。

49816487.article_content:
← Engineering Blog
Tenuo Engineering
·
September 21, 2026
Jev in practice: typed decisions, scoped authority
Building safe agent delegation with Jev, LangGraph, and Tenuo
TL;DR:
safe-upgrade
is a dependency upgrade agent built on Jev, LangGraph, and Tenuo. Jev turns repository evidence into typed probabilistic decisions. LangGraph carries those decisions through a durable workflow. Tenuo gives each resulting action a task-scoped warrant. The design rule: keep judgment, control flow, and authority separate.
We started with a builder’s question: what does a useful workflow look like when Jev, LangGraph, and Tenuo each address a distinct part of the system?
Dependency upgrades gave us a practical way to answer it because, as repository maintainers quickly learn, an apparently mechanical process can conceal difficult compatibility questions. You change a version, install the package, run the tests, and open a pull request, yet the release may have removed an API the repository calls, changed module format, or altered behavior that the existing suite does not exercise. Installation and CI can succeed while the application remains broken.
A useful upgrade agent has to interpret release evidence, relate it to an unfamiliar repository, decide what work is required, change code, and establish that the result is sound. It also receives access to source files, package installation, test commands, Git, and sometimes a remote repository.
This combination let us study both sides of agent development: making useful decisions from messy context and controlling the actions that follow them.
Begin with a decision the program can use
Jev was our starting point because dependency upgrades contain semantic questions that ordinary rules handle poorly:
Does this release note affect the way this repository uses the package?

49817289.article_content:
We noticed builders often wished their Claude Code or Codex setup could run in the cloud because locally their agent idea just “worked” with those harnesses.
But the moment you build your own agent, you’re on your own. It’s tricky wiring up the right primitives just well enough to match that “it just worked” feeling.
Today we’re releasing
Strands harness
: a fully assembled state-of-the-art agent harness you can easily run locally or deploy to your favorite provider. It’s built to be a general-purpose agent rather than a coding agent. All you need is one line of Python or TypeScript to get it working with your choice of model. Strands harness beats other agent harnesses on cost efficiency while maintaining equal or better accuracy. It’s available under an Apache 2.0 license.
Strands harness
costs 28% less
when using the same Claude or GPT models across six benchmarks. We found Strands harness showed better token-efficiency and nearly equal benchmark scores compared to Claude Code, Codex, and other popular harnesses. That’s important because we never want to sacrifice accuracy for lower cost. Deepseek Harness proved to be the most token-efficient overall, however, it typically reported the lowest accuracy scores. Our testing setup was distributed benchmarking on EC2 with Harbor.
With Fable 5, Strands harness
cost 77% less
than Claude Code
and
scored higher
on Terminal Bench 2.1. We’re also pleased to see two other open source harnesses perform similarly well on cost/accuracy against Claude Code.
Strands harness, built on the
Strands Harness SDK
, contains defaults for prompt caching and context management. Our default context management largely drove the token-efficiency and accuracy: tool results over ~1500 tokens get truncated, summarization (compaction) triggers when the context window hits above 85%, and context recovery runs within the loop if there’s an overflow.
Keep an eye out for a follow-up paper from our researchers regarding these benchmarks. In the meantime, we’re excited everyone gets to use these defaults in Strands harness.

49814780.article_content:
Pre-Sales Engineer, North America
About QuestDB
QuestDB is the low-latency time-series database on open formats. It ingests millions of events per second, computes on live data in milliseconds, and keeps years of history queryable: one SQL engine spanning messaging, stream processing and tiered storage, so teams can act on what is happening and learn from everything that happened.
The engine is written in low-latency Java (zero-GC), Rust, C++ and assembly: columnar storage, vectorized and JIT-compiled SQL, streaming materialized views, and an open lakehouse tier on Parquet and Iceberg. QuestDB Enterprise turns a single server into a fully distributed deployment with a multi-tiered lakehouse architecture, ready for mission-critical workloads on the critical path.
Our open-source repository has passed 17k GitHub stars and we're the fastest-growing database in our category. QuestDB runs in production at tier-1 banks, exchanges, trading firms, hedge funds, crypto platforms and energy operators across four continents, and is expanding into robotics, aerospace and Physical AI. We recently won Best Trading Analytics Platform at the TradingTech Summit Europe, the first non-legacy vendor to do so.
Working at QuestDB
We hire talented and passionate people who share our mission to empower developers to solve their problems with data. We are building breakthrough technology to power the infrastructure of tomorrow.
Work with world-class engineers, including two teammates who placed in the top 10 of the One Billion Row Challenge (1BRC).
We invest in a culture that promotes ownership, autonomy and independent thinking.
We have transparent leadership and value employees' strategic input.
Our team is ambitious and tackles the most difficult problems at the deepest data infrastructure layer.
The role
We're hiring a pre-sales engineer for North America to own the technical side of every sales cycle in the region.
You own the technical validation that happens before a deal is signed: discovery, a time-boxed proof of concept with success criteria agreed up front, benchmarks run on the customer's own data that their engineers can reproduce, architecture sign-off and security review, through to the first production workload. You are the engineer in the room when a bank's platform team asks how replication and failover actually work, or when an aerospace team needs rocket telemetry streamed and queried in real time. Most evaluations are for new projects at firms that already run incumbent systems, so much of the work is making the case credible against what they know: the architecture, the numbers, and a plan their engineers believe they can execute.
You work closely with our CEO, who is on the ground in New York, and with the sales team on every deal. You also work directly with our CTO and core engineers on the product, so what you learn in the field goes straight into the roadmap. This is a hands-on individual-contributor role with a lot of customer time and a lot of autonomy.
Responsibilities
Run technical discovery with engineers, architects and quants: what data they have, how much of it, how fast it needs to move, and what it runs on today.
Design and run proofs of concept with written success criteria and a timeline: build the ingestion path, load representative data, design the schema, write the queries, and measure the results.
Own deployment and architecture conversations: sizing, replication and high availability, backup and recovery, BYOC on AWS and Azure, Kubernetes, RBAC, TLS and SSO, storage tiering and Parquet queries.
Deliver demos and technical deep dives that fit the audience, from a two-person quant team to a bank's architecture review board.
Position QuestDB against the incumbent time-series databases with precision: where we win, where we do not, and what a migration really involves.
Answer security questionnaires, RFIs and RFPs, and run vendor due-diligence sessions with customer security and infrastructure teams.
Hand every closed deal over cleanly: what was built, how it is configured, what was promised, and what is still open, so support and engineering can run it from day one.
Turn field work into reusable assets: reference architectures, benchmark reports, migration guides, sample pipelines and demo datasets.
Feed product gaps and customer requests back to the CTO and core engineering with the evidence attached.
Represent QuestDB at meetups, conferences and customer events in New York, Chicago and Toronto.
Requirements
Has run or supported technical evaluations with enterprise buyers, and knows how to define success criteria and hold a proof of concept to them.
Experience in a hands-on role with databases, streaming or data infrastructure, as a pre-sales engineer, solutions engineer, data engineer or software engineer.
Based in New York City, or on the US East Coast and able to be with customers in New York regularly.
Strong SQL and a solid understanding of database internals: storage layout, partition

data.title: Two Git ignore files nobody told me about
data.author: faithraven
data.article_summary: 文章介绍了 Git 除项目内 `.gitignore` 外的两种忽略文件：`.git/info/exclude` 仅对当前仓库生效且不会提交，适合个人笔记、计划等；全局忽略文件（通常为 `~/.config/git/ignore`）对本机所有仓库生效，适合编辑器和系统杂项。它们语法相同，规则只对未跟踪文件有效。使用 Claude Code 时，被忽略的文件默认不会出现在 `@` 文件补全中，但仍可读取。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：如何选择 Git 的不同忽略机制，避免把个人开发环境产生的文件和规则误提交到仓库。

不同观点：
• **反对提交个人规则**：n4bz0r 认为仓库不应了解开发者的编辑器、工具或个人环境；只有团队共同受益的忽略规则才应提交，否则应由个人自行配置。
• **支持使用本地忽略机制**：评论提到 `.git/info/exclude`、`core.excludesFile`（如 `~/.config/git/ignore`）以及全局 ignore，可处理个人文件而不污染仓库；Windows 用户尤其指出本地路径和文档支持不够直观。
• **偏好显式防误提交**：havnagiggle 使用“DO NOT SUBMIT”标记、预提交检查并关闭 Git smart commits，认为即使这些内容出现在 diff 中，也比依赖忽略规则更安全、透明。
• **工具和文档派观点**：有人指出官方文档已清楚说明多种忽略方式，`git check-ignore` 可追踪文件究竟被哪个规则忽略；Magit 则能方便地管理三类机制。
• **其他需求**：psygn89 希望能只排除配置文件中的某些行，而非整个文件；另有人指出被忽略的文件仍可通过 `git add -f` 强制提交。

补充讨论：争议焦点是“个人便利”与“仓库整洁、团队共享”之间的边界；另有 `respectGitIgnore` 拼写修正及对相关功能不熟悉的反馈。

49814432.article_content:
Two git ignore files nobody told me about
Posted on
2026-09-23
::
4
Min Read ::
Source Code
::
claude-code
git
One of my many bad habits is carrying untracked files around in the repositories I work on.
I did learn, some time ago, that those files must never contain secrets, because sooner or later they get committed by mistake. I learned it the easy way, by watching a colleague learn it the hard way: furiously rewriting history to cover his tracks, then rotating cloud credentials in a panic.
These days the untracked files are harmless. Random markdown notes and, more often than not, agent plans. I haven't started committing those yet. They go stale fast, and I'm not convinced they're worth the effort.
So why put up with a permanently dirty working tree? Because until very recently, the only way I knew to ignore a file in git was to add it to
.gitignore
. And
.gitignore
gets committed. That's exactly right for things everyone cloning the repo will have, like the classic
.env
, but pushing the silly filename I picked for my private notes to a remote repository feels unclean. So I did nothing, and the untracked files piled up. About ten plans at the last count.
But then Claude asked, out of the blue, something along the lines of "would you like me to add these files to
.git/info/exclude
?"
Wait, what? What's that?
The three ignore files
It turns out git reads ignore patterns from three places, all with the same syntax.
Where
Who it affects
Committed?
Typical use
.gitignore
, in any directory
Everyone who clones the repo
Yes
Build output and local environments:
target/
,
__pycache__/
,
.venv/
.git/info/exclude
Only this clone
No
Your own scratch files that the project doesn't need to know about
Global excludes file, set by
core.excludesFile
(default
~/.config/git/ignore
)
Every repo you work in, on this machine
No
Editor and OS clutter:
.idea/
,
.vscode/
,
Thumbs.db
,
.DS_Store
The per-repo one,
.git/info/exclude
, is the one I'm giddy about. It lives inside
.git
, so it can't be committed even by accident, and nobody else ever sees it. I'll probably move some things into
~/.config/git/ignore
soon too; editor clutter has no business in any project's
.gitignore
, and yet there it is, in most of them.
Of course, all of this is laid out very nicely in the
official documentation
, if only I'd thought to read it, or even to search for it. I didn't, and I'd wager a small sum that git is the tool most of us learned by accident, some of them fortunate, some less so. Thankfully, this one was the former.
Using them
The two new ones are plain text files that take the same patterns as
.gitignore
. There's no dedicated git command; you just append to them.
Per repo, from the repository root:
echo
'
plans/
'
>>
.git/info/exclude
echo
'
*.notes.md
'
>>
.git/info/exclude
Patterns are matched relative to the repository root, exactly as they would be in a top-level
.gitignore
. The file is usually already there, with a few commented-out examples in it. One catch: in a linked git worktree,
.git
is a file rather than a directory, so the path above won't work. The exclude file lives in the main repository's
.git/info/exclude
and covers every worktree. This resolves to the right file from the main repository and from any linked worktree:
echo
'
plans/
'
>>
"
$(
git
rev-parse
-
-git-common-dir
)
/info/exclude
"
Globally:
mkdir
-
p
~/.config/git
echo
'
.DS_Store
'
>>
~/.config/git/ignore
echo
'
.idea/
'
>>
~/.config/git/ignore
Git reads
~/.config/git/ignore
automatically if it exists (or
$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore
, if you set that variable); nothing to configure. If you'd rather keep it somewhere else, point git at it once:
git
config
-
-global
core.excludesFile
~/.gitignore_global
Whichever file you use,
git status
stops listing the files immediately, as long as they weren't already tracked; ignore rules never apply to tracked files.
A note on Claude Code
Since ignoring agent plans has been the running example: by default, Claude Code leaves ignored files out of the autocomplete you get when you reference a file with
@
, so the moment your plans go into
.git/info/exclude
they vanish from the picker.
To get them back, add this to your
settings.json
(or flip
Respect .gitignore in file picker
in
/config
):
{
"
respectGitignore
"
:
false
}
This is only about the
@
autocomplete. Claude Code can read the files regardless of the setting; it just won't offer them as you type. The
settings reference
has the details.
So yeah, there you go. If, like me, you only knew about
.gitignore
and were skittish about sharing your note-taking habits with everyone on the project, you can now have a clean working tree without feeling exposed.
AI usage disclaimer
English is not my first language, and I'm not a talented writer in any language, so I use AI to polish my writing. The ideas, the setup, the mistakes and the opinions are all mine. They reach the AI as thorough notes in half-broken English, and it fixes the English. It doesn't supply the thinking

• **反对提交个人规则**：n4bz0r 认为仓库不应了解开发者的编辑器、工具或个人环境；只有团队共同受益的忽略规则才应提交，否则应由个人自行配置。
• **支持使用本地忽略机制**：评论提到 `.git/info/exclude`、`core.excludesFile`（如 `~/.config/git/ignore`）以及全局 ignore，可处理个人文件而不污染仓库；Windows 用户尤其指出本地路径和文档支持不够直观。
• **偏好显式防误提交**：havnagiggle 使用“DO NOT SUBMIT”标记、预提交检查并关闭 Git smart commits，认为即使这些内容出现在 diff 中，也比依赖忽略规则更安全、透明。
• **工具和文档派观点**：有人指出官方文档已清楚说明多种忽略方式，`git check-ignore` 可追踪文件究竟被哪个规则忽略；Magit 则能方便地管理三类机制。
• **其他需求**：psygn89 希望能只排除配置文件中的某些行，而非整个文件；另有人指出被忽略的文件仍可通过 `git add -f` 强制提交。

补充讨论：争议焦点是“个人便利”与“仓库整洁、团队共享”之间的边界；另有 `respectGitIgnore` 拼写修正及对相关功能不熟悉的反馈。

data.title: Tokens Too Cheap to Meter
data.author: teoruiz
data.article_summary: 文章指出，机器学习智能的使用成本正以每年数个数量级下降，主要受GPU效率提升、模型能力增强与推理引擎优化推动。未来一两年，LLM将像基础设施一样融入各类计算；未来3—6年，前沿水平模型可能在普通硬件本地运行。届时AI应用瓶颈将从算力和令牌数量转向质量、可及性及实际需求，并引发供需两侧的“杰文斯悖论”。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：LLM推理成本快速下降的真实性、持续性及其对商业模式、硬件产业和数据中心投资的影响。

不同观点：
• **成本将持续下降但有下限**：有人认为效率提升不可能永远指数增长，成熟软件如 grep 的成本可能构成下限；也有人质疑文章比较口径，2025年是完整“智能指数”成本，2026年却是任务加权均价，降幅被夸大。  
• **乐观的降价趋势**：引用 Epoch AI 分析称，达到同等性能的成本在刚成为业界最先进时下降最快，平均每季度降约66%，两年后速度放缓至32%，但总体仍显著下降。  
• **对数据和图表的质疑**：部分评论认为 GPU 图表难以支持明确趋势，回归线未证明不是噪声；H100 四年前与当前硬件效率差距有限，可能反而削弱文章结论。  
• **商业模式存疑**：即使 token 便宜，建设基础设施投入巨大。若资本规模达万亿美元，需每年持续产生超千亿美元自由现金流才能获得10%回报，文章对此缺乏数据和论证。  
• **产业影响分歧**：Nvidia可能继续主导训练，但推理市场竞争更激烈、利润率下降；本地运行前沿模型或导致 GPU、内存和数据中心需求下降。  
• **泡沫与外部性担忧**：有人认为 AI 未必是泡沫，但数据中心可能因效率提升而过度建设并产生“孤儿设施”；同时能源消耗和环境影响或从严重到灾难性。  
• **类比与反例**：有人将“token便宜到无需计量”类比1954年“核电便宜到无需计量”的落空预言。

补充讨论：争议核心是成本下降速度、统计口径及其能否转化为可持续利润；评论也反映出“当前推理成本被补贴、未来涨价”与“价格将低到难以盈利”两种相反预期。

Table of contents
Is this really happening?
Improvements that affect all AI
Improvements that affect hosted AI
Improvements that affect local AI
Improvements that affect specialized use cases
Putting it together
What happens next?
Tokens become cheaper than tool calls
Supply-side Jevons Paradox
How are investors going to make their money back?
Demand-side Jevons Paradox
Optionality
Summary
The price of using machine learning intelligence is decreasing by several orders of magnitude a year and shows no signs of slowing.
We are likely to see LLMs integrated into every part of computing as infrastructure, not just as a product, in the next year or two.
We are likely to see LLMs running locally at current frontier-quality on commodity hardware in the next 3-6 years.
Starting very soon, we are likely to see
quality
and
access
become the limiting factor to AI
1
use, not sheer number of tokens.
Is this really happening?
Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, so I collected a whole bunch of evidence.
AI can be either proprietary (such as GPT-6 Astra) or open weight (such as GLM-5.3-flash).
Open weight models can be either hosted (e.g. by Z.ai) or local.
Generally, models intended to be run locally will be much smaller, such as
Muse Glimmer
or
Qwen3 Coder
.
Improvements in one don't always affect improvements in the others.
Improvements that affect all AI
GPUs
GPUs are getting exponentially more efficient with every generation.
In the graph below (
source
), the X-axis is time and the Y-axis is power efficiency of the GPU itself.
Larger Y-axis numbers mean more efficient.
This is a logarithmic graph, which is to say that a straight line on the graph represents an exponential increase in efficiency.
In this particular case, the logarithm is 1.3, which means efficiency doubles about once every two years.
This is an increase in efficiency that we haven't seen since Moore's Law in the 1960s.
Models
The cost to complete a given task with a model is going down sharply over time.
Models are usually priced per-token.
A "token" is a fragment of a word; it takes about 1.5 tokens to represent a word.
For every token a model reads, and for every token it outputs, the "model provider" (e.g. Anthropic or OpenAI) charges you some fixed amount of money.
The cost per
token
of models is not consistently going down, at least not for the smartest ("frontier") models.
But the cost per
task
is.
Smaller models may cost less per token, but use more tokens overall than a larger model for the same task, because they have to think more or correct their first drafts.
This section is about the cost to complete the task from beginning to end.
The chart below (
source
) shows the "
pareto frontier
" of cost/task at present.
A pareto frontier shows the best
tradeoff
you can get, not just the best in a single category.
Here, our tradeoffs are:
Y-axis: the "quality" of the model (as measured by a suite of benchmarks)
X-axis: the cost to complete those benchmarks
Cost is on a logarithmic scale.
Larger Y-axis and smaller X-axis numbers are better.
This is showing us a wide range of models on the pareto frontier as of 2026.
Towards the top-right we have Claude Fable-5.1 (expensive and intelligent); towards the middle-left we have GPT-5.6 Luna (cheap and less intelligent).
Models below the dotted line are basically not worth considering.
2
Now, look at this chart showing the frontier at the start, middle, and end of
2025
:
The chart shows models are getting smarter
and
cheaper on a per-task basis over 2025.
If you draw a straight horizontal line at basically any task on the Y-axis, the cost to do it at the end of 2025 was cheaper than at the start;
and if you draw a straight vertical line at basically any point on the X-axis, models can do more for the same cost.
Now, compare that 2025 chart to the 2026 chart.
The Y-axis (intelligence) is about the same, with less of a fall-off towards the cheap end.
The X-axis (cost) has gotten
two orders of magnitude cheaper
.
Inference Engines
An "inference engine" is a software package that takes a trained model and an input text and actually runs it on a GPU.
Inference engines are currently immature and improving rapidly.
Currently we're seeing 10%-50% improvements year-over-year, depending on which engine you look at.
There are two benchmarks that are often compared for inference engines:
"offline" (run a bunch of tokens through in one big batch)
and "serving" (you have people sending your server inputs at unpredictable times, and you want to send a response back as quickly as possible).
Serving is getting efficient much more rapidly than offline inference.
All numbers below are for serving workloads, not offline.
vLLM
vLLM
is an open-source inference engine and it's getting more efficient over time.
In the graph below (
source
), the Y-axis is Joules/token, the X-axis is batch size (roughly: "how many inputs are processed in parallel?"), and the blue/red lines are different software versions.
Smalle

data.author: abrax3141
data.article_summary: 该项目是一个基于浏览器的 IBM 1620 Model 2 计算机仿真器与运行环境，旨在复原这款20世纪60年代面向科研工程的十进制计算机及其软件。仓库包含仿真器、网页界面、操作系统和历史软件资料，支持模拟核心内存、指令系统及多种外设。项目还致力于收集和恢复 IBM 1620 软件，采用 MIT 许可证发布。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕IBM 1620展开怀旧回忆与计算机历史的数字化复现。

不同观点：
• [rzzzwilson]分享个人经历：1969年首次编程使用IBM 1620，可能是Model 2。课程提供编码表、McCracken的FORTRAN II教材和习题，但几乎没有额外指导，学生通过打孔卡提交程序，无法直接操作机器，只能隔着玻璃观看。此次经历促使其放弃物理学，最终投身计算机行业，体现早期计算教育的独特方式及其人生影响。
• [abrax3141]强调当代复现与保存：Paul Kimpel制作了基于网页的IBM 1620模拟器，并成功编译运行1963年的IPL-V编译器和运行时环境。用户无需真实硬件即可在浏览器中体验相关系统，项目资料和运行细节可通过GitHub获取。

补充讨论：两条评论形成“亲历历史”与“技术保存”的呼应：前者说明IBM 1620对个人职业选择的影响，后者则通过模拟器降低体验门槛，使这段计算机历史得以延续。评论间没有明显争议，核心差异在于关注个人记忆还是技术复原。

retro-1620
Web-based emulator and operating environment for the IBM 1620 Model-2 computer system.
The IBM 1620 was a 1960s transistorized, decimal, variable field-length, magnetic-core memory computer system designed primarily as an inexpensive solution for scientific and engineering applications. There were two models, the original Model 1 released in 1959, and the object-code compatible but significantly redesigned Model 2, released in 1962. A total of about 2,000 systems were produced, roughly half each Model-1s and Model-2s. IBM supported the system until 1970.
The 1620 used a two-address, memory-to-memory architecture. There were no software-accessible registers. Instructions were a fixed 12 digits, consisting of an operation code of two digits, a "P" address of five digits (usually the destination operand), and a "Q" address or literal value of five digits (usually the source operand). The basic memory size was 20,000 digits, expandable to 60,000 digits. Each digit contained a four-bit binary-coded decimal value, a fifth "flag" bit used for both the arithmetic sign and as a field delimiter, and an odd-parity "check" bit. All arithmetic and data movement was done digit-sequentially.
The Model 1 featured a memory cycle time of 20µs per two digits. Addition and multiplication were done via a lookup table in memory. Hardware division, floating-point arithmetic, and indirect addressing were optional features.
The Model 2 featured a memory cycle time of 10µs per two digits. Many instructions were optimized to process two Q-operand digits from a single memory fetch. Addition was done in hardware, but multiplication was still done by table lookup. Hardware division and indirect addressing were standard features, with floating-point still an extra-cost option. The Model 2 had two additional options, index register address modification (with the index registers stored in memory at 00300-00399, where the Model 1 add table had resided) and support for binary (actually, octal) bit-wise operations, octal/decimal conversion, and binary paper tape I/O.
Initially, the Model 1 supported only paper-tape and typewriter input/output devices, but the 1622 card reader/punch unit (derived from the IBM 1401's model 1402 reader/punch) was made available soon after the initial release. Additional peripherals were the 1443 line printer, 1311 disk drive with removable disk packs, and 1627 plotter. The typewriter, paper tape, punched card, and printer devices supported alphanumeric data in memory as pairs of adjacent digits.
The 1620 was also used as the computing and control component of the IBM 1710 and 1720 process-control systems. When configured for this role, the 1620 supported several additional instructions and a multi-level interrupt system.
The 1620 had a vast collection of IBM-supplied and user-written software. Most programming was done using the SPS assembler or FORTRAN II. For systems with the 1311 disk drive, there was a simple batch operating system known as "Monitor."
The main goals of this project are creation of a web browser-based emulator for the Model 2 variant of the system and recovery of as much software for the system as we are able to find.

MIT License

data.title: The GitHub wiki is an anti-pattern
data.author: ibobev
data.article_summary: 文章认为，GitHub Wiki唯一优势是访问方便，但缺点众多：无法随代码版本管理、克隆项目时不会一并获取、缺乏PR审查、自动检查和定制能力。因此建议将文档放入仓库的/docs目录，借助GitHub Pages发布，并用Wiki页面链接到文档。项目规模扩大后再迁移至独立文档仓库。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕项目文档应采用 Git 仓库中的 `/docs`，还是 GitHub Wiki，以及文档审查、协作、发布和维护成本之间的权衡。

不同观点：
• **倾向与代码同库**：代码、测试和文档放在同一棵树中，便于版本同步、局部修改和代码审查；文档变更能与代码 diff 一起出现，减少文档悄然腐化。Fossil 被认为能更好地实现文档的版本化和浏览。  
• **反对 GitHub Wiki**：Wiki 不随仓库克隆、本地不可用，结构和搜索能力有限，部分内容难以被搜索引擎或 AI 索引；GitHub Wiki 还可能造成厂商锁定。有人认为 `/docs` 可直接通过 GitHub Pages 发布，效果更好。  
• **支持 Wiki 的低门槛优势**：浏览器甚至手机即可编辑，修正错别字和安装环境说明等“小改动”无需 PR、审批和 CI，能让实际使用者更容易反馈和改进文档。  
• **对审查机制的折中看法**：有人认为 Wiki 跳过 code review 会导致错误和过时内容；也有人认为文档走完整 SDLC 周期过于缓慢，团队应缩短审查时间，或对纯 Markdown 修改跳过 CI。  
• **规模与工具问题**：原评论质疑“文档发展后必然要拆成独立仓库”的前提，认为同库有助于避免代理或开发者在指令、文档、注释等多处重复维护同一信息。

补充讨论：评论指出原文对 Wiki 与 `/docs` 的优缺点划分不够清晰；GitHub 的 Wiki、Issues、Discussions 等功能存在重叠，也增加维护负担；Wiki 缺少目录和并行维护多版本的能力。

49815484.article_content:
The “
should I use the wiki or a docs folder on GitHub?
” discussion comes up every 6 months or so, and following Shawn Wang’s
three strikes rule
I thought it was about time I wrote something down about it.
The initial version of this post opened with “You can use the wiki or a
docs
folder for your GitHub project, both are valid choices” but as I wrote more, I realised that there is a single reason to use a wiki, and many more reasons
not
to use the wiki. So many in fact, that I consider
using the wiki on GitHub is an anti-pattern
.
Let’s start with the benefits of using a wiki:
You can get to the wiki contents in a single click from anywhere in the repo
There is no 2.
Really, the only benefit that I’ve been able to find to using the wiki is that it’s always there.
How about the reasons
not
to use the wiki?
Documentation is versioned alongside your code when using the
/docs
folder. If you need to use an old version, the docs are easy to find
The documentation isn’t available locally when someone clones your repo (you can clone the wiki separately, but this is a hidden feature)
Documentation edits get the same treatment as code. They get a full peer review through the pull request process
You can use GitHub Actions to lint your docs using tools such as
Vale
People can work with tooling that they already know (e.g.
vscode
with spellcheck)
Wikis provide limited branding opportunities. They all look pretty much the same
The wiki doesn’t support image uploads, so you have to put images somewhere else anyway
Now that you’re sold on the idea of keeping docs alongside your code, how do you make it easy for people to view them?
Add your docs to your repository in the
/docs
folder. Do
not
use the
gh-pages
branch as this prevents docs being versioned alongside code
Set up a GitHub pages build to publish the docs
If you’re just getting started, I recommend using the
just-the-docs
theme and letting GitHub build and publish your docs
If you prefer to build your own workflow (e.g. using Hugo), you can use
this
GitHub Action to publish the docs
Add a single wiki page directing people to the hosted documentation
Using the
/docs
folder is the highest effort-to-reward ratio option whilst you’re building out a new product. At some point your docs will outgrow a single folder, and then all bets are off. You’ll want a separate repo with its own build process, pull request review guidelines and a whole host of other things. At that point people are already used to working with docs in a repository, and the migration from
/docs
to its own repo should be seamless for your contributors.
Whether you agree or disagree, I’d love to hear your thoughts
on Twitter
49815484.article_summary: 文章认为，GitHub Wiki唯一优势是访问方便，但缺点众多：无法随代码版本管理、克隆项目时不会一并获取、缺乏PR审查、自动检查和定制能力。因此建议将文档放入仓库的/docs目录，借助GitHub Pages发布，并用Wiki页面链接到文档。项目规模扩大后再迁移至独立文档仓库。
49815484.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕项目文档应采用 Git 仓库中的 `/docs`，还是 GitHub Wiki，以及文档审查、协作、发布和维护成本之间的权衡。

不同观点：
• **倾向与代码同库**：代码、测试和文档放在同一棵树中，便于版本同步、局部修改和代码审查；文档变更能与代码 diff 一起出现，减少文档悄然腐化。Fossil 被认为能更好地实现文档的版本化和浏览。  
• **反对 GitHub Wiki**：Wiki 不随仓库克隆、本地不可用，结构和搜索能力有限，部分内容难以被搜索引擎或 AI 索引；GitHub Wiki 还可能造成厂商锁定。有人认为 `/docs` 可直接通过 GitHub Pages 发布，效果更好。  
• **支持 Wiki 的低门槛优势**：浏览器甚至手机即可编辑，修正错别字和安装环境说明等“小改动”无需 PR、审批和 CI，能让实际使用者更容易反馈和改进文档。  
• **对审查机制的折中看法**：有人认为 Wiki 跳过 code review 会导致错误和过时内容；也有人认为文档走完整 SDLC 周期过于缓慢，团队应缩短审查时间，或对纯 Markdown 修改跳过 CI。  
• **规模与工具问题**：原评论质疑“文档发展后必然要拆成独立仓库”的前提，认为同库有助于避免代理或开发者在指令、文档、注释等多处重复维护同一信息。

补充讨论：评论指出原文对 Wiki 与 `/docs` 的优缺点划分不够清晰；GitHub 的 Wiki、Issues、Discussions 等功能存在重叠，也增加维护负担；Wiki 缺少目录和并行维护多版本的能力。

Montreal city council adopts bylaw banning insults against police, municipal employees
Montreal city council has adopted a bylaw to ban people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.
Residents who insult city staff would face fines between $300 and $1,000 for a 1st offence
Erika Morris
·
The Canadian Press
·
Posted: Sep 21, 2026 6:36 PM EDT | Last Updated: September 21
Play
Listen to this article
Estimated 5 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.
Montreal's city hall building is seen here in a photo taken in November 2024.
(Charles Contant/CBC)
Social Sharing
Montreal city council has adopted a bylaw to ban people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.
The debate over the rule lasted over half an hour, with the Official Opposition saying the proposed bylaw was "half-baked." It was adopted with 35 voting in favour and 25 opposed.
"We are being asked to vote now and consult later," said Marie Plourde, leader of the Official Opposition.
Under the bylaw, residents who insult city staff would face fines between $300 and $1,000 for a first offence. Subsequent offences could result in fines up to $2,000.
City officials have not said when they will implement the bylaw.
Yves Francœur, head of the police brotherhood, has said his union's members have been pushing for such a bylaw for years. But lawyers and civil rights groups worry the bylaw could infringe on the constitutional right to freedom of expression.
Other municipalities in the province, including Quebec City, Laval, Longueuil and Sherbrooke, already have similar bylaws.
Police in Quebec municipalities issued thousands of fines for insulting officers
The Canadian Press reported in June that some of these municipalities have issued thousands of fines over the past six years.
"Giving the middle finger, it's not what will give you a ticket," Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said before the council meeting.
"Let's just be honest. There's bigger issues in terms of the attitude of some citizens."
City employees could refuse service
The new Montreal bylaw would ban insults, harassment, threats, abuse and intimidation, as well as offensive and aggressive behaviour.
It also includes provisions saying city employees could refuse to provide services to someone who misbehaves. However, the bylaw doesn't define what could be construed as an insult.
City councillor Carla Beauvais heavily criticized the administration for not providing clear definitions. She also questioned the lack of public consultations.
"A threat can be proven. An offensive word is felt. And how a person feels can vary from one person to another. So where does the offence begin? Where does permissible anger end? The text doesn't say," said Beauvais.
She cited various decisions from the Quebec City municipal court in which judges could not agree on what constitutes an insult, raising concerns that the rule will cause a backlog at the courthouse.
Citizens are concerned, councillor says
Opposition councillor Martine Musau Muele added that council was asked to vote on the rule without adequate information. She said the documents councillors received did not provide statistics and reports to support the need for the bylaw.
She also said the city did not conduct any risk assessment or prove that the measures under the Criminal Code are insufficient to deal with belligerent residents.
"Citizens are extremely concerned. People do not understand the reasoning of the administration. What led you to decide that today, with everything going on, that this is the most optimal move?" Muele said. "This is a draft, not a proposal."
Man who filmed himself insulting SPVM officer facing criminal defamation charges
Suspension of 4th Montreal officer in racism scandal renews calls for independent probe
The two councillors also raised concerns around giving police more powers while public trust is fragile.
In June, Montreal police disbanded a night patrol unit in the multicultural neighbourhood of
Montréal-Nord
over allegations of racism and misconduct.
Mayor acknowledges concerns
During council, Martinez Ferrada acknowledged that "there will be more questions around this bylaw in the coming months" but insisted the administration "needed to act." She said the administration would make reports publicly available.
She said she "understands the concerns," and "shares some of them." However, she said incidents of inappropriate behaviour have increased dramatically and are harming city employees, and making it more difficult to recruit new employees.
"We are simply saying that there is a line between challenging an institution and engaging in behaviour that is inappropriate toward the people who work for it," said the mayor.
"The thousands of women and men who work every day to serve Montreal have the right to protection fr

data.title: Samsung accidentally freezes its smart fridges with a software update
data.author: Markoff
data.article_summary: 三星因测试系统错误，向韩国部分智能冰箱推送了有问题的SmartThings更新，导致冰箱断电、屏幕和自动开门功能失灵，食物变质。三星已暂停更新并采取紧急维修措施，部分主板被更换。事件再次凸显联网家电的软件风险，用户也要求赔偿损失。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：智能家电是否值得使用，以及联网、可靠性、隐私和耐用性之间的冲突。

不同观点：
• 反对智能家电者认为，冰箱、恒温器等应首先完成基本功能，不应依赖网络、更新或订阅；断网导致设备失效就是设计失败，“能正常制冷”比智能功能更重要。  
• 可靠性与耐用性担忧：评论提到食物甚至药品可能因故障变质；老冰箱使用40多年仍能工作，而增加技术并未显著延长寿命，反而带来“变砖”风险。  
• 隐私和商业模式批评：智能模块可能用于监视、广告或厂商控制；有人认为交易完成后厂商便不再负责，联网生态和集中化趋势不利于用户。  
• 较温和的观点认为智能功能确实提供便利，但在低价市场（如印度）并不普及，说明成本尚未被消费者认可。  
• 个别评论将问题归因于韩国品牌，认为其暗黑模式尤其严重；也有人以《硅谷》、广告冰箱等玩笑调侃。

补充讨论：争议焦点是“便利功能”能否抵消可靠性、隐私、维护成本和使用寿命的代价；主帖中断开无线模块后冰箱仍正常运行，强化了“非必要联网”的批评。

Samsung accidentally freezes its smart fridges with a software update
Another reason to think twice about buying a connected appliance.

TL;DR
Samsung has halted a SmartThings update to smart fridges in Korea after some owners reported that their fridges stopped working.
Samsung confirmed the issue and said it was taking “emergency measures.”
This latest issue once again highlights the risks associated with using connected appliances.
There are plenty of
smart home
appliances on the market, featuring internet connectivity, cross-device integration, and a host of other features. However, there’s no shortage of horror stories about these connected appliances failing. Now, we can add another Samsung smart refrigerator issue to the list.
Samsung has stopped rolling out a SmartThings update to its smart refrigerators in Korea after some owners reported major issues,
ZDNET Korea
reports. More specifically, many users on
Samsung’s Korea Community
forum report that their fridges completely stopped working, resulting in spoiled food. Other issues include the automatic door-opening function not working and the fridge’s internal lights not turning on.
A Samsung representative confirmed the issue on the
company’s forum
:
Yesterday (9/22), an error occurred during the testing process for a Samsung refrigerator software update.
Abnormal symptoms have been observed in the refrigerator power and screen of some customers.
We are currently taking emergency measures as a top priority through Samsung Electronics Service Centers.
The fact that this issue apparently occurred while Samsung was testing a software update for the fridges is very concerning. It raises the question of how a work-in-progress software update found its way onto users’ fridges in the first place.
ZDNet Korea
suggests that the update was pushed out to users due to a “system error.” A Samsung representative also told the outlet that it had stopped distributing the update.
Samsung has advised affected customers to contact its service center. We’ve also seen user reports that company technicians have been replacing the motherboard inside these faulty fridges. However, many customers have also urged Samsung to compensate them for the spoiled food. This issue couldn’t have come at a worse time for Korean users, as the country celebrates the Chuseok holiday on Friday.

data.title: The Price of Intelligence Is Falling Rapidly
data.author: gotmedium
data.article_summary: Epoch AI报告显示，过去三年，达到同等AI性能的成本平均每季度下降47%，即每年降低约13倍，速度超过历史上其他变革性技术。例：OpenAI o3到GPT-5.6 Luna在相近成绩下，成本18个月内下降约725倍。AI不仅更聪明，也更便宜，这或削弱开源模型对前沿模型的威胁。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕“智能价格快速下降”的AI报告，评论者争论其概念是否成立、AI能力与人类智能的区别，以及由此带来的社会后果。

不同观点：
• 质疑报告及其表述：报告来自Epoch AI，虽获独立基金支持，但有人认为Tabarrok对其缺乏批判；“智能价格”这一单位本身也可能只是营销说法。  
• 认为下降的是人工智能服务成本，而非人类智能价值；真正被压低的可能是生活水平、劳动价格和受教育者的议价能力。有人担忧资本将人类智能商品化，最终只剩“愚蠢的权力”。  
• 反驳“智能变便宜”适用于所有领域：文本生成成本或许下降，但图像、语音、嵌入模型并未同步进步。  
• 强烈批评AI可靠性：LLM依赖概率、训练数据和不可验证的封闭系统，无法承担责任；代码、艺术和决策应由可追责的人完成并保留人的署名与成就。  
• 担忧AI被不合格者滥用，像“不会木工却拿着电动工具”，可能降低黑客和寻租成本，激化社会冲突。  
• 另一方认为成本下降有利于利润增长；也有人指出AI仍需高水平人类提供材料和指导，否则能力会停滞。

补充讨论：争议焦点是“智能”究竟指人类能力、AI输出质量，还是可购买的服务；同时涉及效率提升与责任、尊严、阶层利益之间的冲突。
